title: 3 questions that can help universities turn AI experiments into results
summary: Explore how AI in higher education can help leaders connect institutional intelligence, build trust, and turn experimentation into measurable impact.
body_markdown:
Higher education institutions don’t need another conversation about whether AI matters. The more important question now is how to turn growing experimentation into meaningful, measurable progress across the academic mission.


In our recent Microsoft Education Blog post, “[Higher education’s AI advantage is the intelligence institutions already hold](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/education/blog/2026/09/higher-educations-ai-advantage-is-the-intelligence-institutions-already-hold/) ,” we introduced a simple idea: a university’s greatest AI advantage may not be access to another model or tool. It may be the unique intelligence already held across its people, data, research, systems, policies, and everyday work.


**Now comes the harder question: how do institutions put that intelligence to work?**


Our new guide,[How to Unlock Intelligence in Higher Education](https://info.microsoft.com/ww-landing-higher-education-how-to-unlock-intelligence-in-higher-education.html?LCID=EN-US) , is designed to help leadership teams move from AI experimentation toward impact at scale. It provides a practical framework, built around priority AI use cases, for bringing leaders together around three critical conversations: where AI can advance university priorities, what information needs to be connected, and how to build the trust needed to innovate responsibly.


[Download How to Unlock Intelligence in Higher Education](https://info.microsoft.com/ww-landing-higher-education-how-to-unlock-intelligence-in-higher-education.html?LCID=EN-US)


## Start with university priorities, then scale the AI use cases that advance them


Across higher education, faculty, staff, researchers, and students are already exploring AI. Connecting those experiments to shared priorities is what turns them into university-wide transformation.


A more useful starting point is the mission.


- Which outcomes is the university trying to improve?
- Where are people spending time on work that creates friction rather than value?
- Where might better access to university knowledge improve a decision, experience, or workflow?


This frames the conversation around “What are we trying to achieve, and which AI use cases can help us get there?” Use cases give universities a repeatable pattern to adapt and scale.


Take academic advising: AI can help advisors see where each student stands in their degree progress and reach out sooner, while advisors remain responsible for the conversation. A university can prove that pattern in one college, then scale it across campus. For more examples across teaching, research, student experience, operations, and cybersecurity, explore the white paper:[Empowering Every Leader and Learner: AI Use Cases in Higher Education.](https://info.microsoft.com/ww-landing-empowering-every-leader-and-learner-in-higher-education.html?lcid=en-us)


Answering that question requires more than IT leadership. The guide encourages institutions to bring together executive and academic leaders, faculty, research, student services, legal and compliance, IT and cybersecurity, finance, operations, and administration. That multidisciplinary conversation matters because university intelligence doesn’t sit neatly inside one system or organizational function. It exists across the university.


The guide organizes that work into three conversations. Each one builds on the last: where AI can make the greatest difference, what intelligence needs to be connected, and what will let people innovate with confidence.


## Conversation 1: Where could AI make the greatest difference?


The first conversation is about focus. Many institutions have already accumulated promising pilots. The next opportunity is to connect those experiments to university strategy and identify where AI can make a meaningful contribution to priorities like student success, academic work, research, operations, and university effectiveness.


Start with outcomes rather than capabilities.


- Where could reducing administrative burden give faculty and staff more capacity?
- Where could faster access to trusted information improve a student’s experience?
- Where could AI augment a research or institutional workflow while keeping people responsible for judgment and decisions?


Research is a good place to see this in practice. Microsoft worked with the Research Data Alliance and researchers worldwide to identify[Global Community Priorities for Agentic AI in Research](https://zenodo.org/records/18184204) and outline a[Data Director Agentic AI Tool Blueprint](https://zenodo.org/records/22275620) that shows how agents can support research workflows.


This is also an opportunity to look across existing AI activities. Universities can ask what their teams are learning from experimentation, which approaches could be reused, and where separate initiatives might become more valuable if connected.


The objective is to apply AI where it can contribute most meaningfully to the university’s mission.[The University of South Carolina shows](https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/25399-university-of-south-carolina-microsoft-365-copilot/) what AI can deliver when aimed at increasing capacity for high-value work. Following the deployment of[Microsoft Copilot](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/education/products/copilot-in-education) and AI agents in the tools people use every day, 84% of pilot users reported saving one to five hours per week, and eight in 10 reported satisfaction. That reclaimed time is capacity the university can direct toward teaching, research, and student success. Realizing that value at scale depends on giving AI access to the right university knowledge and context, which leads to the second conversation.


[Explore Microsoft Copilot in education](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/education/products/copilot-in-education)


## Conversation 2: What intelligence needs to be connected?


Once priorities are clearer, a second question quickly emerges: What does AI need to know to be genuinely useful in the context of our institution?


Every university possesses a distinctive body of intelligence: academic programs and curriculum history, student records and outcome patterns, research data and intellectual property, faculty and staff expertise, policies and governance, operational processes, and information contained in documents, meetings, messages, and decisions. Too often, that intelligence is fragmented across systems and organizational boundaries.


Connecting fragmented information can help AI deliver more relevant, consistent results across workflows rather than requiring each agent to reconstruct context independently.


This is where[Microsoft IQ](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/ai/microsoft-iq) becomes important. Microsoft IQ is designed to provide a shared intelligence layer that helps Copilot and agents use context about how people work, how the university operates, and what it knows.


- [Fabric IQ](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-fabric/features/iq) establishes consistent definitions, relationships, metrics, and rules so AI can reason with university context across its data.
- [Work IQ](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/copilot/features/work-iq) brings real-time context from everyday activities, collaboration, relationships, and workflows across[Microsoft 365](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/) , including what needs attention.
- [Foundry IQ](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/ai-foundry/iq) makes knowledge from connected sources accessible through governed, reusable knowledge bases for AI applications and agents.
- And[Web IQ](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/webiq) adds timely, relevant context from the web, such as news, images, and videos.


Together, these capabilities help AI deliver more relevant, consistent results across university workflows while working with existing security, identity, and governance controls.


Making the right knowledge available in the right context, with appropriate permissions and governance, helps people make better-informed decisions and lets AI support more useful workflows.


[Discover Microsoft IQ](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/ai/microsoft-iq)


## Conversation 3: What will allow people to innovate with confidence?


There is one more conversation institutions cannot separate from AI transformation: trust.


As AI and agents become part of everyday university work, leaders need to consider governance, security, privacy, compliance, academic integrity, and human accountability from the beginning. That doesn’t mean governance should put the brakes on innovation. Done well, governance creates the conditions for innovation.


People are more likely to explore valuable applications of AI when they understand which information an AI system can access, what it can do, where human review remains essential, and what safeguards protect institutional, research, employee, and student data.


This becomes even more important as institutions move from AI that helps people create and analyze information toward agents that can participate in longer, multistep workflows.


The University of Kentucky shows what this looks like when trust is established from the start. When leaders took inventory of AI activity, they found more than 150 separate initiatives already underway. Its[CATS AI governance framework](https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/26551-university-of-kentucky-microsoft-365-copilot) brought them together under one university-wide approach, and more than 70,000 students and employees now have access to Microsoft Copilot.


The lesson is important: trust creates the foundation for people to experiment, build, and innovate responsibly at scale.


## From conversation to action


These three conversations are interconnected. Start with the university outcomes that matter. Identify the knowledge, data, and expertise required to make progress. Then create the governance and trust that allow people and AI to work with that intelligence responsibly.


The conversation itself can also become a source of intelligence. The guide includes a practical approach for using Microsoft Copilot to synthesize notes from leadership discussions, identify recurring themes, and surface emerging priorities and possible next steps.


The universities that lead in the next phase of AI will likely be those that connect AI with their own knowledge, people, data, workflows, and purpose, securely and responsibly.
